## Example: The inclusion $\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ in the category of (unital) rings

Let $\mathbf{Ring}$ be the category of unital rings with unital ring homomorphisms, and let $f = i: \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ be the canonical inclusion.

### Claim 1: $i$ is an epimorphism.

We must show $i$ is right-cancellative: for any ring $R$ and any homomorphisms $g, h: \mathbb{Q} \to R$, if $g \circ i = h \circ i$ (i.e., $g|_{\mathbb{Z}} = h|_{\mathbb{Z}}$), then $g = h$.

Take any $p/q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p, q \in \mathbb{Z}$, $q \neq 0$. Since $g$ and $h$ are unital homomorphisms,

$$g(q)\cdot g(1/q) = g(1) = 1 \quad\text{and}\quad h(q)\cdot h(1/q) = h(1) = 1,$$

so $g(1/q)$ is the multiplicative inverse of $g(q)$, and $h(1/q)$ is the multiplicative inverse of $h(q)$. But $g(q) = h(q)$ (as $q \in \mathbb{Z}$), and inverses in a ring are unique, so $g(1/q) = h(1/q)$. Therefore

$$g(p/q) = g(p)\,g(1/q) = h(p)\,h(1/q) = h(p/q).$$

Hence $g = h$, and $i$ is an epimorphism. $\checkmark$

### Claim 2: $i_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}: \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q})$ is not surjective.

The induced map sends $\alpha: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z}$ to $i \circ \alpha: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}$.

**The codomain is nonempty:** $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}} \in \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q})$.

**The domain is empty:** There is no unital ring homomorphism $\alpha: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Indeed, any such $\alpha$ must send $1 \mapsto 1$, hence $n \mapsto n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. In particular $\alpha(2) = 2$. But then

$$\alpha(1) = \alpha\!\left(2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \alpha(2)\,\alpha(1/2) = 2\,\alpha(1/2),$$

so $2\,\alpha(1/2) = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, which is impossible. Hence $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) = \varnothing$.

Since the domain is empty but the codomain contains $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}}$, the map $i_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}$ cannot be surjective: $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ has no preimage.

### Conclusion

We have exhibited a category ($\mathbf{Ring}$), an epimorphism $i: \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$, and an object $C = \mathbb{Q}$ such that the post-composition map

$$i_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}: \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q})$$

is not surjective (its domain is empty while its codomain contains $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}}$). This shows that epimorphism (right-cancellativity) does **not** imply that the induced map on $\mathrm{Hom}(C, -)$ is surjective for every $C$ — surjectivity of $f_{*}^{C}$ for all $C$ is the stronger condition of $f$ being a **split** epimorphism (a section-retraction), which is strictly stronger than being an epimorphism.

### PROOF COMPLETE

$$g(q)\cdot g(1/q) = g(1) = 1 \quad\text{and}\quad h(q)\cdot h(1/q) = h(1) = 1,$$

so $g(1/q)$ is the multiplicative inverse of $g(q)$, and $h(1/q)$ is the multiplicative inverse of $h(q)$. But $g(q) = h(q)$ (as $q \in \mathbb{Z}$), and inverses in a ring are unique, so $g(1/q) = h(1/q)$. Therefore

$$g(p/q) = g(p)\,g(1/q) = h(p)\,h(1/q) = h(p/q).$$

Hence $g = h$, and $i$ is an epimorphism. $\checkmark$

### Claim 2: $i_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}: \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q})$ is not surjective.

**The codomain is nonempty:** $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}} \in \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q})$.

**The domain is empty:** There is no unital ring homomorphism $\alpha: \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Z}$. Indeed, any such $\alpha$ must send $1 \mapsto 1$, hence $n \mapsto n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. In particular $\alpha(2) = 2$. But then

$$\alpha(1) = \alpha\!\left(2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \alpha(2)\,\alpha(1/2) = 2\,\alpha(1/2),$$

so $2\,\alpha(1/2) = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, which is impossible. Hence $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) = \varnothing$.

Since the domain is empty but the codomain contains $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}}$, the map $i_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}$ cannot be surjective: $\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{Q}}$ has no preimage.

### Conclusion

We have exhibited a category ($\mathbf{Ring}$), an epimorphism $i: \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}$, and an object $C = \mathbb{Q}$ such that the post-composition map

$$i_{*}^{\mathbb{Q}}: \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Z}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{Q})$$
